performers: Musopen Symphony (Commons credit; ensemble attribution disputed)
intro: The violas begin this Andante with repeated notes, and the violins join them one group at a time. The little figures that flutter between its phrases grow surprisingly fierce in the middle.

sections.label: A · Violas begin, violins answer
sections.mNote: Repeated notes climb through the strings in E♭ major

cues.title: The violas start it
cues.text: The violas repeat a note; second violins join above them, then first violins higher still. Each part starts before the previous one has finished. A melody grows out of these overlapping entries, with the woodwinds adding their own replies.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), II, bars 1–8. The order of entries is also described by Marianne Williams Tobias, Indianapolis Symphony Orchestra: https://www.indianapolissymphony.org/backstage/program-notes/mozart-symphony-no-40/.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Three symphonies in a summer
cues.text: Mozart enters his last three symphonies in his own catalogue on 26 June, 25 July and 10 August 1788: the E♭ major, this G minor work and the Jupiter. All three are dated within forty-five days.
cues.evidence: Mozart’s own thematic catalogue (British Library, Zweig MS 63, https://searcharchives.bl.uk/catalog/040-001945812), as listed in the chronological table in Otto Jahn, Life of Mozart, trans. P. D. Townsend (1882), vol. 3: K. 543 on 26 June, K. 550 on 25 July, K. 551 on 10 August 1788. https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/43413

cues.title: Quick notes between phrases
cues.text: Tiny, quick figures slip between the longer notes in strings and winds. They give the Andante a nervous edge: even its most graceful phrases have something stirring underneath.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), II, bars 20–32, with the short figures exchanged between strings and woodwinds.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ten days at home
cues.text: In Vienna on 27 June 1788, Mozart writes to Michael Puchberg from his new lodgings: “In the ten days I have lived here I have worked more than in two months at the other place.” He asks his friend to visit. He is always at home.
cues.evidence: Mozart to Michael Puchberg, 27 June 1788, Bauer–Deutsch 1079, lines 23–25. Our translation of the German transcription, Digital Mozart Edition: https://dme.mozarteum.at/DME/objs/raradocs/transcr/pdf/BD_1079.pdf.

cues.title: The small figures bite
cues.text: The development takes up the repeated notes and the quick string figures. Sharper harmonies and strong wind chords make them sound newly insistent. Mozart keeps the Andante pace; the agitation comes from what the parts do inside it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), II, development, bars 53–73.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: E♭ and the opening phrase
cues.text: The repeated-note phrase returns in E♭ major, rebuilding the melody through the strings. The quick interjections return too. Mozart brings home both the tune and the things that have been worrying it.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), II, recapitulation from bar 74.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A second wind section
cues.text: Mozart revisits the symphony and adds two clarinets, rewriting the oboe parts around them. Both versions survive: the same string-led Andante with two different wind ensembles.
cues.evidence: The two versions are printed in the Breitkopf & Härtel score (1880) and listed at https://imslp.org/wiki/Symphony_No.40_in_G_minor,_K.550_(Mozart,_Wolfgang_Amadeus).

cues.title: Musopen’s Kickstarter
cues.text: Musopen, a nonprofit founded by Aaron Dunn in 2006, raised more than $68,000 on Kickstarter in 2010 to record public-domain classics that anyone may use freely. This movement is among the results; Commons credits the players only as “Musopen Symphony”.
cues.evidence: Jim Farber, “Musopen: Will This Site Set Music Free?”, San Francisco Classical Voice, 25 September 2012 (Dunn and 2006; Kickstarter contributions of $68,630 from 1,276 backers): https://www.sfcv.org/articles/feature/musopen-will-site-set-music-free. Seattle Star, 2012: a $10,000 request that received $68,360: https://www.seattlestar.net/2012/08/musopen-sets-music-free/. The recording’s Commons page files it under the category Musopen Kickstarter Project and credits “Musopen Symphony”: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Mozart_-_Symphony_No._40_in_G_minor,_K550_-_II._Andante_(Musopen_Symphony).flac

transitions.title: Repeated notes after the B♭ cadence
transitions.to: Dev · Quick figures against wind chords
transitions.how: The exposition closes in B♭ major. The strings restart the repeated-note figure, then quick string runs meet stronger wind chords. The tempo stays Andante while chromatic notes pull the phrase away from the settled cadence.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), II, bars 51–65.

transitions.title: The string phrase finds E♭
transitions.from: Dev · Quick figures against wind chords
transitions.to: A′ · Repeated notes return in E♭
transitions.how: The development subsides into short woodwind replies above the strings. The repeated-note opening then returns in E♭ major, with the string entries overlapping again. Its familiar rhythm survives the change from the middle’s crowded exchanges to the quieter opening phrase.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score (1880), II, bars 66–81.

source.title: Mozart, Symphony No. 40, K. 550, Breitkopf & Härtel, Mozarts Werke VIII/40 (1880), plate W.A.M. 550; parts common to both versions
source.locator: II. Andante, PDF pp. 19–29: opening imitative entries, wind replies, development and return. The edition prints both orchestral versions.

timeline.note: Violas begin the repeated-note figure; second and first violins take it up in turn.
Horns support the violins’ melody above the moving lower strings.
Short wind figures answer the strings’ phrases.
Repeated string notes alternate with fuller wind-and-string phrases in the development.
Quick string figures move against held wind chords.
The repeated-note opening returns, passing upwards through the strings.
Full orchestral phrases alternate with quieter string replies before the E♭ major close.

composer.background:
When Leopold Mozart arrived in Vienna on 11 February 1785, the copyist was still writing out his son’s new concerto for that evening’s concert at the Mehlgrube. Wolfgang had been so busy supervising the copying that he had found no time to try the finale through. This was K. 466 in D minor: restless, syncopated strings, then a piano entering with a tune of its own. Leopold thought the concert splendid.

The next day, Haydn heard three quartets at Wolfgang’s home. Leopold recorded his verdict in a letter to Nannerl begun on 14 February: “Before God, and as an honest man, I tell you that your son is the greatest composer I know, personally or by name.” Haydn praised his taste and his knowledge of composition. Mozart would dedicate the quartets to him.
